sections.label: Extending Act against gangs
sections.summary: The Act deals with egregious criminal activities, especially gangs and secret societies, and this Bill extends it for another five years.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: The Act is a critical piece of legislation for us to deal with egregious criminal activities which threaten the sense of safety and security in Singapore, in particular the activities of gangs and secret societies.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: This Bill seeks to extend the Act for another five years.

sections.label: Orders issued under Act
sections.summary: From 21 October 2019 to 31 December 2023, 123 persons were dealt with under the Act, with 86 Detention Orders and 37 Police Supervision Orders issued.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: From 21 October 2019 to 31 December 2023, 123 persons were dealt with under the Act – 86 Detention Orders (DOs) and 37 Police Supervision Orders (PSOs) were issued.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: Even so, the number of orders issued is significant and the Act continues to be necessary and relevant – not only against secret societies, but also other criminal activities, such as unlicensed moneylending.

sections.label: Gangs intimidating witnesses online
sections.summary: Gangs have used technology and social networking sites such as X, Instagram and Facebook to intimidate witnesses.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: Gangs have also used technology and social networking sites, such as X formerly known as Twitter, Instagram and Facebook, to intimidate witnesses.

sections.label: Incident on 9 November 2021
sections.summary: One incident took place on 9 November 2021 at about 4.00 am.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: One incident took place on 9 November 2021 at about 4.00 am.

sections.label: Seven gang members dealt with
sections.summary: Seven of the gang members were dealt with under the Act.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: Seven of the gang members were dealt with under the Act.

sections.label: Detaining unlicensed moneylending syndicate leaders
sections.summary: In 2019, the Act was used to detain leaders and financiers of an unlicensed moneylending syndicate linked to more than 1,800 harassment cases.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: In 2019, we used the Act to detain a number of leaders and financiers of an unlicensed moneylending syndicate, which was linked to more than 1,800 cases of harassment of debtors in Singapore.

sections.label: Detention order numbers falling
sections.summary: Detention orders issued fell from 97 in 2019 to 80 in 2022.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: As was mentioned by the hon Minister of State, the numbers of detentions have come down.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: I looked at it: in 2019 it was 97 detention orders issued; 2022, 80 detention orders.

sections.label: Global Organised Crime Index report
sections.summary: A 2023 report states foreign criminal actors operate in Singapore with moderate influence, mostly in immigration crimes, money laundering and scams.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Apart from what the hon Minister of State highlighted in this House, I note with concern that it is stated in the Global Organised Crime Index Report on Singapore for 2023 that foreign criminal actors continue to operate in Singapore with and, I quote, "moderate influence", and almost all of them are involved in immigration-related crimes, money laundering and scams, amongst others.

sections.label: Extending the Act
sections.summary: The speaker is convinced it is in Singapore's better interest that the Act be extended.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: On balance, I am convinced, based on the hard facts that have been laid out in this House by the hon Minister of State, that it is in the better interest of Singapore that the Act be extended.

sections.label: Secret society entry age
sections.summary: A study the speaker was involved in found secret society entry age ranged from 11 to 18.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: In the study that I was involved in, it was noted that the entry age for secret society members ranged from as young as 11 to 18.

sections.label: Median age of DOs and SOs
sections.summary: The Minister said the median age of persons subject to DOs and SOs from 2017 to 2019 was 22, with the youngest 17.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: In answer to a Parliamentary Question (PQ) I filed in October 2020, the hon Minister for Home Affairs revealed that the median age of persons subject to DOs and SOs between 2017 and 2019 was only 22.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: He also stated that the youngest persons subject to these orders were 17.

sections.label: No recruitment DO or SO case
sections.summary: The speaker's research found no case where the Minister's power was invoked to impose a DO or SO for secret society recruitment activities.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: From my research, though, I have not been able to unearth any case where the power of the Minister was invoked to impose a DO or SO against a person for conducting recruitment activities for a secret society per se.

sections.label: Porting and repealing Parts
sections.summary: The Government should consider porting Parts 2, 3 and 4 to other legislation and then repealing these Parts in this Act.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Respectfully, I think the time has come for the Government to consider porting over Parts 2, 3 and 4 to other pieces of legislation and then repealing these Parts in this Act.

sections.label: Secret society recruiters and Public Order Act
sections.summary: Relevant provisions could be ported to the Public Order Act 2009, and recruiters of youths into secret societies should face the full force of the law.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: In the alternative, there may also be a case to port over relevant provisions to the Public Order Act 2009 which is the primary piece of legislation that the Government relies on to regulate and control assemblies to maintain public order.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: It is sad that there continues to be cases of youths falling victim to the machinations of secret societies.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: We should call out the acts of recruiters and bring to bear the full force of the law against them either by prosecution under the Societies Act or through the exercise of the powers under this Act.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: It is these recruiters who seduce vulnerable and immature young people by making false promises of charmed and privileged lifestyles.

sections.label: Resolute action against recruiters
sections.summary: More resolute action against recruiters would help turn young people away from crime and violence toward their own bright futures.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Through more resolute action against the recruiters, I believe we will have a far better chance of turning our young people away from dark alleys of crime and violence and instead focus on the flourishing of their own bright futures, for their sake, that of their families as well for Singapore.

sections.label: Minister's power to order detention
sections.summary: Under this Act, the Minister may, with the Public Prosecutor's consent, order detention of a person for up to 12 months in the interests of public safety, peace and good order.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
sentences.text: Under this Act, the Minister can, with the consent of the Public Prosecutor, order the detention of a person for any period not exceeding 12 months, if the Minister is satisfied that it is necessary that the person be detained in the interests of public safety, peace and good order.

sections.label: Detention and Police supervision numbers
sections.summary: The speaker asks the Minister of State for the total number of people detained under the CLTPA and subject to Police supervision under it since October 2019.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
sentences.text: The Minister of State has also highlighted some of the recent serious cases in the past five years which required enforcement under CLTPA.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
sentences.text: I would also like to ask the Minister of State, in the last five years, since October 2019, what is the total number of people who, one, have been detained under the CLTPA and two, have been subject to Police supervision under the CLTPA?

sections.label: Five-year extension, no amendment
sections.summary: In today's Second Reading, the Government seeks a five-year extension of the Act and proposes no amendment to the current Act.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
sentences.text: In today's Second Reading, the Government is asking for a five-year extension of the Act and no amendment of the current Act is being proposed.

sections.label: MHA press release on Act
sections.summary: MHA stated the Act is an essential legal instrument for Police against secret societies and criminal syndicates, and has been used since 2019 to detain or supervise persons.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
sentences.text: In the Ministry of Home Affairs' (MHA's) press release dated 7 March 2024, in respect of the First Reading of today's Bill, it was stated that the Act is, I quote, "an essential legal instrument for the Police so that they can act effectively against secret societies and criminal syndicates, such as moneylending and drug-trafficking syndicates, where prosecution is not viable because witnesses are unwilling to testify in open Court for fear of reprisal." MHA stated that since 2019, the Act has been used to detain or place under supervision persons heavily involved in secret society activities and leaders of organised crime syndicates, such as an overseas licensed moneylending syndicate.

sections.label: Question on CLTPA renewal conditions
sections.summary: A Member asked the Minister of State what conditions or goals would give confidence to consider not seeking further CLTPA extensions.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
sentences.text: In recent years, we have also received assurances from Minister that the number of detainees under the CLTPA have been declining.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
sentences.text: As we review the need for a renewal of the CLTPA today, for the next five years, I would therefore like to ask the Minister of State what would be the conditions or goals, the attainment of which may grant confidence to our Government to consider not seeking further extensions in future.

sections.label: Former Minister on doing away
sections.summary: The then Home Affairs Minister said the Act can be done away with when secret society and drug traffic components are reduced to small proportions.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
sentences.text: The then Home Affairs Minister answered as follows, and I quote, "Mr Shanmugam asked: when can we do away with it?

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
sentences.text: My answer to that would be, we can do away with it when we are satisfied that both the secret society component of our objective and the drug traffic component of our objective are reduced to such small proportions that we can safely say that we do not need this to control both aspects." The Minister then went on to elaborate on his views.

sections.label: PSP safeguard on Supreme Court Judges
sections.summary: The PSP's first proposed safeguard is to legislatively require that sitting Supreme Court Judges sit on the Advisory Committees.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: The PSP's first proposed safeguard is to legislatively require that sitting Supreme Court Judges sit on the Advisory Committees.

sections.label: Consent for DO or PSO
sections.summary: Besides the Public Prosecutor's consent, the Minister must seek the Advisory Committee's concurrence or the President's concurrence before a DO or PSO is made.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Besides the Public Prosecutor's consent, the Minister must also seek either: one, the Advisory Committee’s concurrence; or two, the concurrence of the President, acting in his discretion, before the DO or PSO is made.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: If an Advisory Committee objects to the extension of the DO or PSO and the Government disagrees, any extension should only be granted with the President's concurrence, acting in his discretion.

sections.label: PSP opposes CLTPA extension
sections.summary: The PSP will oppose the CLTPA extension unless safeguards are enhanced; the Bill renews the Act for the 15th time.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: In light of these considerations, the PSP will oppose the extension of the CLTPA, unless the safeguards are enhanced.

sentences.speaker: Mr Speaker
sentences.text: Sitting accordingly suspended at 3.10 pm until 3.30 pm.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: This Bill will renew the Criminal Law (Temporary Provisions) Act for the 15th time.

sections.label: Police Supervision Order obligations
sections.summary: The passage states the speaker's first point concerns obligations imposed on persons subject to Police Supervision Orders under section 33.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: My first point is on the obligations imposed on persons subject to Police Supervision Orders under section 33.

sections.label: Three types of Advisory Committees
sections.summary: The passage states Advisory Committees check broad Act powers, with three types reviewing Detention Orders and Police Supervision Orders, annual detainee cases, and detention beyond 10 years.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: The Advisory Committees are an important check on the broad powers under the Act.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: There are three types of Advisory Committees: the first to review every Detention Order (DO) and Police Supervision Order (PSO); the second to review every detainee’s case at least once annually; and the third to review detention cases for extension beyond 10 years.

sections.label: Recidivism rate question
sections.summary: The passage asks whether the Minister of State can share the recidivism rate of individuals subject to Detention Orders and Police Supervision Orders.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Can the Minister of State also share the recidivism rate of individuals subject to DOs and PSOs?

sections.label: Powers under the Act
sections.summary: The passage states the Act lets the Minister for Home Affairs authorise detention without trial for certain suspected crimes and gives police related powers.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Specifically, the Act allows the Minister for Home Affairs to authorise the detention without trial of someone suspected of being involved in, or with, certain crimes, including drug trafficking, homicide, gang rape, armed robbery, syndicated crime organisations, illegal money lending and people trafficking.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The Act also gives police the authority to arrest and detain a person without a warrant, restricts the manufacture and possession of documents considered to be subversive and restricts strikes and lock-outs that might disrupt or prevent the delivery of essential services.

sections.label: Concerns about detention without trial
sections.summary: The passage states removing the Act may carry a price, and some Singaporeans are concerned about Executive-authorised detention up to 12 months without trial.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: However the price we may pay if we remove it may not be a price Singaporeans or Singapore is prepared to pay.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: There is considerable and understandable concern among some Singaporeans about an Act that allows the Executive to authorise the detention of a person for up to 12 months without trial, with some people potentially thinking that we are arbitrarily detaining people for no good reason.

sections.label: Information for routine public release
sections.summary: The passage lists information that should routinely be public, including numbers detained, reasons, detainee age and sex, order outcomes, day release, and appeals.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Other information that should routinely be made available to the public includes the number of people detained per year, and the reason for their detention; the age and sex of the detainees; the number of detention orders confirmed, cancelled, or extended by the President every year; the number of people on day release to attend employment; and, the number of successful and unsuccessful appeals.

sections.label: Detainees' prison facilities and recidivism
sections.summary: The speaker seeks clarification on whether detainees share prison facilities and programmes with sentenced inmates, and on their recidivism rates.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In light of the above, I would welcome clarification that those detained under this Act are housed in the same prison facilities as those sentenced through the regular court system, and have access to the same rehabilitation and reintegration services and programmes.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I would also welcome clarification about the number of people who have been detained under the Act who have subsequently reoffended post release, and how these recidivism rates compare to the general prison population.

sections.label: Inmates with gang affiliations
sections.summary: Singapore Prison Services states close to one quarter of inmates entering prison in 2021 had gang affiliations.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In fact, according to Singapore Prison Services, close to one quarter of the inmates who entered prison in 2021 had gang affiliations.

sections.label: Need for the Act
sections.summary: The Act remains necessary while crime threatens Singapore's safety, but must be used responsibly, accountably and only as a last resort.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In an ideal world, there would be no need for this Act, however while national and international crime continues to pose an identifiable threat to one of the defining characteristics of Singapore, our safety and security, the need for this Act remains.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: It is, however, beholden on us, as Members of Parliament, to ensure that this Act continues to be used in a responsible and accountable manner and only as a last resort.

sections.label: Act extended 14 times
sections.summary: The Act has been extended 14 times, most recently in 2018.

sentences.text: The Act has been extended 14 times, the last being in 2018.

sections.label: Rioting and secret society cases
sections.summary: The Minister said an average of 112 rioting and serious hurt cases yearly were linked to secret societies over five years.

sentences.text: Minister further said that an average of 112 rioting and serious hurt cases have been linked to secret societies in Singapore each year, for the past five years, and cases involving the use of weapons, such as parangs and knuckle dusters have declined over that same period.

sections.label: Loan shark and drug offences
sections.summary: Minister Shanmugam cited 1,587 unlicensed moneylending cases from April to August 2020 and about 6,000 drug abusers arrested yearly in the 1990s.

sentences.text: For illegal loan shark activities, in an October 2020 reply to a PQ, Minister Shanmugam said that between April and August 2020, there were 1,587 cases of unlicensed moneylending and unlicensed moneylending-related harassment reported.
Next, for drug related offences, in a 2022 Committee of Supply debate, the Minister informed this House that in the 1990s, the Central Narcotics Bureau arrested about 6,000 abusers per year.

sections.label: Criminal Law (Temporary Provisions) Act safeguards
sections.summary: The speaker says the law balances due process with law and order, citing safeguards including public prosecutor consent, Supreme Court Judges chairing advisory committees, annual reviews and a five-year sunset clause.

sentences.text: To me, and I reiterate, that this is all about striking the right balance between having the right to due process versus the need to maintain law and order in Singapore.

I perused the Hansard in respect of the 2018 debate on extension of this law and having read about our six safeguards listed by the Minister for Home Affairs, I am sufficiently convinced that we do have a robust process, to ensure that any decision made by the Minister to detain a person without trial, is carefully scrutinised and assessed.
In particular, I am of the view that having the consent of the public prosecutor before the making of a detention order is an important requirement.

The next safeguard is having sitting Judges of the Supreme Court of Singapore chair the advisory committee, and that is another key factor that persuaded me, that any person detained under this law, where the sufficient safeguards to ensure that there is a strong basis for the detention order.
And these orders will be reviewed annually, by different advisory committees, which will be chaired by different Supreme Court Judges.
And the final safeguard that I am satisfied with is the fact that Parliament has to review the necessity of this law every five years, due to the expiry date or the sunset clause of this law.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, since the enactment of the Criminal Law (Temporary Provisions) Act in 1955, it has proven itself essential and effective in empowering the Police to act against crime syndicates and secret societies.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: The prosecution of their cases is challenging, due to reasons, such as reluctant witnesses.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: In fact, I believe a lot of my Parliamentary colleagues in this House would have similar experiences with their residents, who are willing to provide information, but request to not disclose their identity, out of fear and for their safety.

sections.label: New Zealand youth gang increase
sections.summary: New Zealand saw a 75% increase in youths aged 18 to 25 joining gangs between 2017 and 2022.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
sentences.text: New Zealand has also seen a 75% increase in the number of youths aged from 18 to 25 years old, joining gangs between 2017 and 2022.

sections.label: Detainee statistics and detention duration
sections.summary: The Singapore Prisons Service publishes annual detainee statistics, 123 persons were dealt with under the Act from 21 October 2019 to 31 December 2023, and no detainees are currently detained more than 10 years.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
sentences.text: That said, the Singapore Prisons Service (SPS) publishes statistics on detainees annually and I would refer Mr Tan to those annual statistics.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
sentences.text: I have also stated, in my opening speech, that 123 persons were dealt with under the Act from 21 October 2019 to 31 December 2023.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
sentences.text: There are currently no detainees who have been detained for more than 10 years.

sections.label: Detention orders against recruiters
sections.summary: Detention orders have been and will continue to be issued against recruiters.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
sentences.text: DOs have been and will continue to be issued against recruiters.

sections.label: Advisory Committees assess cases
sections.summary: Advisory Committees assess each case on its own merits and may summon and examine a witness under section 40 of the Act if deemed necessary.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
sentences.text: The Advisory Committees assess each case on its own merits, and exercise their powers under section 40 of the Act to summon and examine a witness, if they deem it necessary.

sections.label: Public Defender's Office aid to detainees
sections.summary: Detainees are currently not assigned counsel by the state, in response to Mr Leong's question on whether the Public Defender's Office will extend aid to them.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
sentences.text: As for Mr Leong's question, as to whether the Public Defender's Office will extend aid to detainees, detainees are currently not assigned counsel by the state.

sections.label: Prison Yellow Ribbon work opportunities
sections.summary: Prison collaborates with Yellow Ribbon Singapore to provide detainees with work opportunities.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
sentences.text: For instance, Prison collaborates with Yellow Ribbon Singapore to provide detainees with work opportunities.

sections.label: Razwana asks about recidivism rate
sections.summary: Assoc Prof Razwana asked about the recidivism rate of detainees compared to the general prison population.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
sentences.text: Assoc Prof Razwana asked about the recidivism rate of detainees, as compared to that of the general prison population.

sections.label: Act powers safeguard public safety
sections.summary: The powers under the Act will ensure the continued safeguard of public safety, peace and good order in Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
sentences.text: The powers under the Act will ensure the continued safeguard of the public safety, peace and good order in Singapore.

sections.label: PSP support with safeguards adopted
sections.summary: PSP would in principle support the Bill if its recommended safeguards are adopted.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: In principle, PSP would like to support the Bill if our recommended safeguards are adopted.

sections.label: Annual reviews no minimum period
sections.summary: There will be annual reviews and there is no minimum period.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
sentences.text: As I shared earlier, there will be annual reviews, there is no minimum period.

sections.label: Case specific reviews of provisions
sections.summary: Detention is case and detainee specific, no one will be detained beyond what is necessary, and provisions will continue to be reviewed.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
sentences.text: So, it is very case specific, detainee specific.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
sentences.text: However, we feel that we will not detain anyone beyond what is not necessary.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
sentences.text: With regard to your second question, as I replied to Mr Murali earlier, we will continue to review these provisions and propose changes, if necessary.
